name: Per-feature dictionary diagnostic scatter
summary: A scatter in which every point is one learned feature, placed by numbers read off its own encoder and decoder vectors — how concentrated its direction is in the neuron basis, its bias, its decoder-encoder dot product, its density. It is for claims about a whole dictionary made before anyone has interpreted a single feature.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Both figures make a claim about a whole dictionary at once, and must make it before anyone knows what a single [[feature]] means. The only inputs are the autoencoder's own weights: per feature, one column of the [[dictionary-decoder]] and one row of the [[autoencoder-encoder]]. No tokens, no activations, no human reading examples — cheap enough to run over every feature, which is what a claim about the population rather than about chosen cases needs.

A summary number was available each time and would have hidden the point. In the replication, the reported split — 4% of features dominated by one neuron, 4% by their top ten, 92% neither — is the table version. The scatter shows those labels are threshold cuts through one continuous cloud, not three kinds of thing. In the density appendix an average is the wrong instrument: the claim is that two groups exist, and a mean sits between them. Two axes would not serve either — the third diagnostic is added because no one of the three separates the groups alone.

### How to read it, step by step

One point is one feature: one hidden unit of the [[sparse-autoencoder]], placed by numbers computed from its own weights.

In the decoder-sparsity version, square every entry of the feature's decoder column ([[feature-direction]]) and divide by their sum. The x-axis is the largest single share; the y-axis is the shares ranked two through ten, added. Both are fractions of the same total, so $x + y \le 1$; none of the next nine can beat the top one, so $y \le 9x$ — the straight diagonal edge cutting the upper left. Colour is a label the author assigned by thresholding those same shares (red 1-sparse, green 10-sparse, blue dense) — his reading drawn onto the plot, not a second measurement; the cutoffs are not printed. Read the marginal histograms first: the scatter overplots worst where most features are.

In the three-diagnostic version, depth is [[feature-density]] as $\log_{10}$, running $-10$ to $-3$, logged because densities span that many orders of magnitude. Height is the feature's entry of the encoder bias $\mathbf{b}_e$ inside $\mathrm{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$, always negative and readable as a firing threshold. The horizontal axis is the dot product of the decoder column with the encoder row, which carries information only because the two are learned independently ([[untied-decoder-weights]]). Colour re-encodes depth. Look at the shape of the cloud, not where any point sits: the claim is only that one compact blob stands clear of the mass.

### What a bad result would look like

If features were mostly neurons under another name, the decoder-sparsity cloud would pile against the right edge — $x$ near 1, $y$ near 0, the top marginal spiking there. Instead the blue mass sits below $x = 0.2$, the bulk form of what the case studies find one feature at a time ([[neuron-basis-coefficients]], [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]]) and what [[superposition]] predicts. Note the plot does not display the claim attached to it — that the [[privileged-basis]] survives anyway, by the [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test]]; that comes from the text, not the figure.

For the three-diagnostic version, failure is a gradient rather than an island: orange shading continuously into crimson with no gap, which is what density alone gives in large runs with a large [[l1-coefficient]] ([[feature-density-histogram]]). One rendered angle can also mislead: a projection may open a gap that closes on rotation, and the reader gets one view. And separation, however clean, does not show the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] is a training artifact ([[density-cluster-separation]]); it supplies a boundary to draw, no more, and the paper says only that the cluster "appears to be" one.

### Where it comes back

Twice, in different hands. Figure 63 sits in the [[external-replication]] section: two axes plus marginals, categorical colour, an outsider's dictionary from a different one-layer model, asking whether features are neurons. Figure 66 sits in the density appendix: three axes, continuous colour, the authors' own run, asking whether the [[high-density-cluster]] can be fenced off — its darkest points, the rarest, being [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]. The habit carries across both: a point is a feature, its coordinates come from weights alone, and the evidence is where the cloud sits.
